name: Corporatism
summary: Corporatism organises society and the economy through recognised functional bodies, syndicates of workers and employers joined in corporations, that cooperate under public authority instead of competing as classes or as a free market. Its Catholic form (Leo XIII, Pius XI) defends private property under duties to the common good and a family wage, and rejects both liberal competition and socialism; its state form (Italy's Labour Charter, Salazar's 1933 constitution) made the syndicates and corporations organs of the State, banned strikes and gave them a part in representation.
scope: Classical corporatism: Catholic social teaching as set out in Rerum novarum and Quadragesimo anno, and the corporative state as it was written into law in fascist Italy (the 1926 law and 1927 Labour Charter) and in Salazar's Portugal (the 1933 constitution, a corporative republic), the cases the scholarship names (Schmitter, Schneider, Gallagher). Answers rest on those texts and on the record of those regimes' corporative order, not on their general policies. It excludes postwar democratic neo-corporatism, modern state-corporatist systems outside the interwar cases, and the unrelated sense of rule by large corporations. Of Portugal's 1933 constitution, only what it calls corporative answers (article 5's corporative republic, article 34's corporative economy, the corporations of Title IV and the Corporative Chamber); its family articles and the State's general tasks are the Estado Novo's other positions (coatrack correction, 2026-11-14).
